title: Music (5 min max) — the stories behind the tracks

facts: Alice Merton wrote 'No Roots' after moving house around 12 times by age 24 — the song came from realising she had no single place to call home, before concluding her real home is with the people she loves.
While recording, Merton noticed the wordless 'ooh' hook sounded too much like Maroon 5's 'Moves Like Jagger,' so she and her producer reworked the melody to make it distinct.
No label would release it her way, so Merton put it out on her own imprint, Paper Plane Records — a name nodding to M.I.A.'s 'Paper Planes.'
In February 2018 'No Roots' hit No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Songs chart, making Merton only the ninth woman in a lead role to top that chart since it began in 1988.
As the song broke in the US, she performed it on 'The Late Late Show with James Corden' — a belated American push over a year after its European release.

The lyric is about feeling your own problems are trivial: the narrator measures his everyday struggles against a grandfather who landed at Normandy and a firefighter father, and feels he has no right to complain.
The title comes from the sarcastic 'world's smallest violin' put-down — mocking self-pity — a phrase popularised by a 1978 episode of M*A*S*H.
Despite the mocking title, a real, regular-sized violin is played on the track by Danny Ferenbach; the stacked vocal harmonies were partly inspired by The Beach Boys' 'Barbara Ann.'
It became a delayed hit after going viral on TikTok in 2022, where users paired its 'blow up' line with clips of their own content going viral.
It reached only No. 91 on the Hot 100 but climbed to No. 10 on Hot Alternative Songs, and was certified Platinum by the RIAA in December 2024.

Though it's a K-pop hit, 'Cupid' was written and produced by a European team (Swedes Louise Udin, Mac Felländer-Tsai and Adam von Mentzer); the English 'Twin Version' is sung by members Sio and Aran about a girl's unrequited love.
It became the first song by a K-pop girl group to reach the UK Top 10 (No. 8), and its 10-week Hot 100 run (peak No. 17) was the longest for any K-pop girl group.
A sped-up edit of the 'Twin Version' topped TikTok's global chart for 2023 with over 20 million video creations, and it was the most-viewed song page on Genius that year.
In August 2023 an official new version arrived featuring Sabrina Carpenter, who added her own verse about heartbreak and regret.

The rookie group from tiny label Attrakt scored a shock global hit, but at its peak all four members filed a court injunction to suspend their contracts, triggering a bitter legal battle that fractured the group.

JAWNY wrote and produced 'Honeypie' himself as an independent, no-label release in April 2019, building its sweet, funky 'nu-disco' sound around the honey/honeypie metaphor for the giddy pull of young love.
The song blew up on TikTok in 2019, becoming JAWNY's first mainstream hit and leading directly to him signing with Interscope Records in January 2020.
'Honeypie' has racked up over 270 million Spotify streams and is certified Platinum in the US, Platinum in Canada and Silver in the UK.
JAWNY started as a one-man bedroom operation, self-recording and self-producing the track before any label was involved — hence the comparisons to lo-fi acts like Mac DeMarco and Beck.
Pub-quiz gold: JAWNY first recorded as 'Johnny Utah,' named after Keanu Reeves' character in Point Break, and during 'Honeypie's rise he dated Doja Cat — another artist on this very playlist.
'Fire for You' is about the ache of being magnetically drawn to someone you know is bad for you — the 'on fire' image works as both the thrill of new passion and the burn of having to walk away.

A true slow-burn: released in 2019, it only broke big after a 2020 Netflix sync, eventually reaching No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart in early 2021 and earning an RIAA Platinum certification.

Cannons multi-instrumentalist Paul Davis played keyboards, drums and bass and also engineered, mixed and mastered it himself, sliding between a Fender jazz bass and a Novation synth for that hypnotic groove.
The big break came when it soundtracked a scene in Netflix's teen comedy 'Never Have I Ever' in 2020, topping The Hollywood Reporter's Top TV Songs chart for that May.
Dance superstar Tiësto released an official remix of 'Fire for You' in July 2021, pushing the indie synth-pop track onto dance floors worldwide.

Doja Cat says 'Go To Town' came together fast over a simple beat; she admits she Googled words that rhyme with 'incredible' (which she calls 'cheating') and that on a couple of lines she genuinely doesn't know what she meant.
'Go To Town' was the lead single and opening track of Doja Cat's 2018 debut studio album 'Amala.'
It was co-produced by Yeti Beats — Doja's longtime go-to producer and a former punk-rock guitarist — alongside Rogét Chahayed and Rian Lewis.
The music video, directed by Jabari Jacobs, leans into Doja's cat persona, featuring her posing with Bengal kittens.
Loaded with cheeky double entendres, it's one of Doja Cat's most explicit early songs and helped cement the playful, unapologetically raunchy style that became her signature.
'Big Energy' interpolates Tom Tom Club's 1981 classic 'Genius of Love' — the exact same source Mariah Carey built her 1995 hit 'Fantasy' on, which is why the two songs sound like cousins.
Songwriter Theron Thomas originally wrote 'Big Energy' for Cardi B, but it ended up going to Latto instead.
The track became Latto's first Billboard Hot 100 top-10, peaking at No. 3 in 2022, and is certified 4x Platinum by the RIAA.
Its live version earned Latto a 2023 Grammy nomination for Best Melodic Rap Performance, and it won Song of the Year at the 2022 BET Hip Hop Awards.
A March 2022 remix teamed Latto with Mariah Carey and DJ Khaled, weaving in Carey's 'Fantasy' — a full-circle loop back to the 'Genius of Love' sample both songs share.

'Deadwood' is the work of Really Slow Motion, an epic trailer-music house founded in 2013 by Agus Gonzalez-Lancharro, who builds the label's cinematic tracks with a rotating pool of 200+ composers worldwide.

It lived for years as a YouTube-only track; after being flooded with daily messages asking why it wasn't streamable, Really Slow Motion finally released it to Spotify and stores in April 2021 by popular demand.
'Deadwood' is a staple of the fan-made and indie trailer scene on YouTube, powering countless dramatic edits and short-film trailers.

The studio behind it is a heavyweight of the trailer world: Really Slow Motion's catalogue has been licensed for the campaigns of major films including Solo: A Star Wars Story, A Quiet Place and Deadpool 2.
Despite the label's ironic name, 'Deadwood' is a driving, roughly three-minute epic dark-rock action instrumental engineered to score high-adrenaline, apocalyptic trailer moments.

Although Anne-Marie sings it and Coi Leray raps it, the song was co-written by Ed Sheeran with his regular hitmakers Johnny McDaid and Steve Mac — the same team behind Anne-Marie's earlier hits '2002' and 'Beautiful.'
The whole track is built on Haddaway's 1993 Eurodance smash 'What Is Love,' a song that reached No. 1 in 13 different countries.

The Hannah Lux Davis-directed video winks at the 1998 comedy 'A Night at the Roxbury,' with clubbers doing the Butabi brothers' famous head-bob — fitting, since 'What Is Love' was that film's running gag.
The single scored a Grammy nomination for Best Pop Dance Recording — the first-ever Grammy nods for both Coi Leray and Anne-Marie.
It doubled down on a formula that had just worked for Guetta: a year earlier his 'I'm Good (Blue)' with Bebe Rexha revived Eiffel 65's 1998 hit 'Blue (Da Ba Dee)' in exactly the same way.
There are no outside instruments here: Pogo built the entire song from tiny snippets — single words, notes and sound effects — chopped out of Disney's 1951 'Alice in Wonderland.'
Uploaded on 18 July 2007 as Pogo's very first YouTube video, 'Alice' became his breakout viral hit and is still one of his most-watched, with tens of millions of views.
Disney was so struck by the remix that it flew the young Australian out to the Pixar campus, where he met Toy Story director John Lasseter and Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull.
Disney first had the video pulled for copyright infringement — then turned around and signed Pogo to a one-year contract making music for its studios.
Pogo works in a style called plunderphonics: he records small sounds, quotes and melodies from a single film and sequences them into an entirely new piece of music.

The song opens with Bad Bunny narrating how his parents met: his father 'Tito,' a truck driver from Vega Baja who'd dreamed of being an engineer, met his mother 'Lisy' while helping a friend move house — which is where the title, 'The Move,' comes from.

Beneath the family story it's a political statement, referencing Puerto Rico's 1948 'Gag Law' that once made displaying the Puerto Rican flag a crime, and name-checking 19th-century independence thinker Eugenio María de Hostos.
The closing track is a salsa dura tribute that samples Bad Bunny's own 2020 song 'P FKN R.'

The video — co-directed by Bad Bunny and Janthony Oliveras and released on his birthday, 11 March 2025 — is packed with Puerto Rican symbolism, from the light-blue independence flag to nods to the 1868 Grito de Lares revolt.
It closes his 2025 album 'Debí Tirar Más Fotos,' won Best Urban Song at the 2025 Latin Grammys, and climbed back up the Hot Latin Songs chart after his Super Bowl halftime performance.

The beat stitches together an unlikely trio of samples: Peaches' raunchy 'F*** the Pain Away,' Julie Andrews and Dick Van Dyke's 'Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious' from Mary Poppins, and the kids' singalong 'If You're Happy and You Know It.'
Yung Gravy produced the track together with acclaimed dance-music producer Valentino Khan.
A playful hook name-dropping a girl called Tracy turned the song into a TikTok sensation, inspiring thousands of user videos.
Released as the final single from his 2020 album 'Gasanova,' 'oops!' was certified Gold in the US and bubbled under the Hot 100.
Weeks after release, a remix retitled 'oops!!!' arrived with a guest verse from rap legend Lil Wayne.
Every sound in 'Wishery' is lifted from Disney's 1937 'Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs,' with the wishing-well song 'I'm Wishing' and the dwarfs' 'Heigh-Ho' the most prominent building blocks.
Pogo constructed the track's drum groove out of animal noises pulled straight from the film.
Released in November 2010, the remix quickly racked up millions of YouTube views.
Pogo actually made 'Wishery' while under contract to Disney — yet when he posted it publicly he openly expected the studio to sue him for it.
He also released a companion experimental B-side called 'Digery,' assembled from the same Snow White footage.
Asadov released 'Flying' on the Mark Music Records label on 31 May 2025, filed by dance stores under Deep House.
The Original Mix runs about 4:25 at 118 BPM in the key of A major.
'Flying' proved popular enough to spawn official reworks — a Javid Remix and a HilalDeep Remix both followed on Mark Music Records in June 2025.
The stores can't quite agree on its genre: Beatport files 'Flying' under Deep House while Traxsource lists it as Melodic / Progressive House.

The title 大展鴻圖 isn't slang — it's a classic four-character Chinese idiom, an auspicious blessing meaning roughly 'may your grand ambitions unfold,' the kind of phrase written on scrolls to wish someone success in a new business or the new year.

Beneath the phonk bass, the track opens by sampling a performance of the beloved Cantonese opera 'The Flower Princess' (帝女花) — the grainy, distorted vintage texture of that opera vocal is a deliberate part of the song's sound.
The song helped rocket producer Skai Isyourgod past 3 million monthly Spotify listeners in July 2025, making him the most-streamed Chinese artist on the platform that month.

The video was shot across Hong Kong — including racehorses thundering down the Hong Kong Jockey Club track and the century-old Lin Heung Tea House — and features Zac Purton, one of Hong Kong racing's most successful jockeys, as a symbol of success.
The lyrics are a tongue-in-cheek satire, painting exaggerated, humorous portraits of a nouveau-riche lifestyle and its showy displays of wealth in modern China.

L'Impératrice was founded in 2012 by keyboardist Charles de Boisseguin as an all-instrumental project in Paris, and 'Vanille Fraise' (French for 'strawberry vanilla') comes from those early wordless years, released in 2015.

The track dates from the band's instrumental period, before singer Flore Benguigui became their face — the funky French nu-disco sound honed here grew into the breakout that later put them on stages like Coachella.

'Vanille Fraise' is a purely instrumental cut driven by a funky bassline and silky synths, powered by the group's original lineup of two keyboardists, a bassist, a guitarist and a drummer — no vocals needed.

The video stages a sun-drenched summer sports match between a white team and a pink team that descends into chaos once a strawberry-vanilla ice cream gets involved — a playful, Wes Anderson-tinged bit of whimsy.
The whole groove is built on a sample from a 1970s soul record: Anita Ward's 1979 track 'Spoiled by Your Love' — from the same album as her one global smash, 'Ring My Bell.'

Ren doesn't just cover the song — he grafts on his own original rap verse painting modern working-class Britain, from a night out on your last tenner to funerals and dead-end jobs, threaded through with the refrain 'as above, so below.'

Ren Gill is a fiercely independent Welsh artist with no major label — months after his 2022 mental-health epic 'Hi Ren' went viral, his album 'Sick Boi' crashed in at No. 1 on the UK Albums Chart in October 2023.

The original Verve strings aren't the Rolling Stones themselves — they came from a 1965 orchestral cover of the Stones' 'The Last Time' by the Andrew Oldham Orchestra, which arranger Wil Malone then re-recorded at London's Olympic Studios.

Ren's video plays as an ode to Britain — he walks the streets of his home turf rapping to camera, echoing the original 1997 clip where Richard Ashcroft strode down a London street barging past passers-by.

Because of that string sample, The Verve were forced to hand 100% of the songwriting royalties to Jagger, Richards and manager Allen Klein's ABKCO — until 2019, when Jagger and Richards voluntarily signed the rights back to Ashcroft.

The featured voice belongs to Crista Ru of the duo POWERS, who began as behind-the-scenes songwriters — penning tracks for Selena Gomez, Kylie Minogue and Christina Aguilera — before 'Classic' became their own breakthrough.
Released in September 2014 through Neon Gold and Big Beat, 'Classic' was a deliberately funkier, more disco-leaning turn for The Knocks and served as the lead single of their 'So Classic' EP.
The music video is a live-action recreation of the video game The Sims 4 and doubled as official marketing for the game, flipping the cliché summer 'pool party' pop video on its head.

The Knocks got their name from angry neighbours: their studio monitors were so loud in a paper-thin-walled New York apartment that people kept banging on the walls — they called it 'getting the knocks.'
In March 2016 the song was re-released with a new rap verse from 'Trap Queen' star Fetty Wap, giving 'Classic' a second life as part of The Knocks' debut album '55.'
The song was written by the legendary husband-and-wife team Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, the same pair behind 'You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'.'
Despite heavy US Top 40 radio play, the single only reached No. 36 on the Hot 100 and was seen at the time as a commercial disappointment for Cass Elliot, then newly solo after The Mamas & the Papas.
Cass Elliot's version was released in September 1969 on Dunhill Records and produced by Steve Barri, part of her run of solo singles after the group split.

The song became iconic through 'Lost': in the Season 2 premiere, Desmond plays it on a record player inside the hatch, only for the needle to be knocked off when the hatch is blown open — a scene that drove its 21st-century rediscovery.
Cass wasn't the first to record it: a vocal trio called the Will-O-Bees released the original version in 1968, but it went nowhere before she turned it into a standard.
In a neat coincidence, this track called 'Emotion' is built around a sample of the group The Emotions — specifically their 1976 disco cut 'I Don't Wanna Lose Your Love.'
The sampled original was produced by Earth, Wind & Fire mastermind Maurice White and arranger Charles Stepney, so the club groove sits on a genuine 1970s Chicago soul foundation.
Purple Disco Machine is Tino Piontek from Dresden, Germany, a leading figure in the modern disco revival who won a 2023 Grammy for his remix of Lizzo's 'About Damn Time.'
'Emotion' is essentially a sample-flip instrumental rather than a track with a new guest singer — the soulful vocal hook is lifted from The Emotions' original recording.
The track exemplifies Piontek's signature blend of disco, house and funk, made for the dance-floor during the disco sound's return to clubs that he says transformed his career.
BoA co-wrote 'Woman' with Jon Hume, Hookman and Ivy Adara, and Hume produced it; she wrote six of the album's ten tracks herself, making it one of her most hands-on records.
The song is a deliberate empowerment anthem: BoA said it condemns pitting women against each other and urges listeners to set their own standards of beauty rather than society's.
'Woman' launched BoA's first Korean-language full-length album since 2015's 'Kiss My Lips,' and the record peaked at No. 6 on South Korea's Gaon albums chart.
The choreography went viral for its opening 'upside-down walk,' and the video deliberately features women of different ages, body sizes and racial backgrounds.
Rolling Stone India later named 'Woman' among the ten greatest feminist songs in K-pop, and the album was nominated for Best Pop Album at the 2019 Korean Music Awards.
Brody Dalle wrote 'Don't Mess With Me' as a defiant survivor's anthem, alluding to hardships she'd come through including addiction, abuse and the break-up of her band The Distillers.
It was the third single from 'Diploid Love,' Dalle's first solo album after fronting The Distillers and Spinnerette; the album drew a four-star Rolling Stone review.
The track was produced by Dalle with Alain Johannes, the Queens of the Stone Age collaborator known for his work with Chris Cornell and Them Crooked Vultures.
In the video, Dalle keeps playing her Telecaster while being pelted with pills, powder, fake blood, flour and birthday cake — objects chosen to visualise her refusal to be knocked down.
The song found a second life in gaming: it plays on the car radio in an episode of 'Life is Strange: Before the Storm,' reaching a whole new audience of players.
'Mrs. Hollywood' isn't about a real person — it paints a partner so consumed by chasing fame in California that she's perpetually 'MIA,' with the narrator left waiting for her attention.
The song exploded on TikTok through Go-Jo's street-busking clips; a video of him performing it at Sydney's Bondi Beach has been watched more than six million times.
'Mrs. Hollywood' racked up around a billion cumulative views across video platforms and helped make Go-Jo one of Australia's most-streamed artists of 2023.
Go-Jo — real name Marty Joe Zambotto — grew up off-grid on a remote Western Australian estate with no mains electricity, the family running on solar panels wired to recycled car batteries.
On the strength of his viral rise, Go-Jo went on to represent Australia at the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest in Basel — not with 'Mrs. Hollywood' but with a different song, 'Milkshake Man.'
Nile Rodgers personally recommended Janelle Monáe for the track after the band wanted a guest voice on the chorus; Monáe recorded her parts in Los Angeles.
The vocal session was lightning-fast — drummer Roger Taylor recalled that John Taylor and Simon Le Bon flew over, cut their parts in what felt like a few hours, and flew straight back.
'Pressure Off' was the lead single from 'Paper Gods,' Duran Duran's 14th studio album and their first new record in five years, released in September 2015.
The upbeat video was directed by Nick Egan and shot in Los Angeles and London, with Nile Rodgers and Janelle Monáe joining the four band members on screen.

It reunited the band with a longtime ally: Nile Rodgers had co-produced their 'Notorious' album and remixed their US No. 1 'The Reflex' — and here co-writer Mark Ronson worked with Rodgers for the first time.

The song began by accident: Sofi Tukker's Sophie Hawley-Weld broke her leg on stage at Australia's Groovin The Moo festival, and while stuck recovering at home she wrote the skeleton of a track about being confined indoors.

A song literally about being locked inside was released just as the world went into COVID lockdown — a coincidence the duo called a 'happy accident,' turning it into an unintentional isolation anthem.
Sofi Tukker finished the idea with UK house duo Gorgon City and put it out on Ultra Music, keeping it alive by DJing it on daily lockdown livestreams rather than on tour.
The official video is built entirely from fan-submitted clips of people dancing in quarantine — footage from the 'Freak Fam' gathered across 118 days of Sofi Tukker's daily livestream DJ sets.
Framed as a defiant club track for people stuck at home, the pair's message was that being under 'house arrest' didn't stop them going to the club in their minds.
Despite sharing its title with Loverboy's 1981 rock classic, MAX's 'Working For The Weekend' is a completely original song, not a cover — a coincidence of names, not an interpolation.
MAX and AJR wrote it together as a love letter to hustle — about the late nights, early mornings and never being able to switch off when you're chasing what you're passionate about.
Fittingly for a song about overwork, MAX and rapper bbno$ hammered out his guest verse back-and-forth on a Saturday — a day they were both supposed to be taking off.
The track was produced by pop trio AJR, whose signature stamp is all over it — the brassy trumpet stabs and rhythmic clicks are pure AJR studio style.
It landed as the second track on MAX's September 2020 album 'Colour Vision,' with MAX noting he'd toured and been 'in the trenches' with AJR for years before they made it together.

This is a bossa-nova cover of Coldplay's 'Clocks' — and the original almost never came out: Chris Martin knocked out the piano riff and most of the words in about 15 minutes late in the sessions, and the band nearly shelved it.

Coldplay's original is a rare Grammy giant that flopped on the charts — reaching only No. 29 in the US and No. 9 in the UK, yet still beating OutKast's 'Hey Ya!' and Beyoncé's 'Crazy in Love' to Record of the Year at the 2004 Grammys.
The hypnotic, cascading piano arpeggio this bossa version slows down was inspired by the band Muse; U2's Bono was so taken with it he praised its 'Philip Glass-type arpeggiation.'

Ituana is an Argentine lounge/bossa-cover project whose version of the Rolling Stones' 'You Can't Always Get What You Want' closed the Big Little Lies season-one finale — the episode that won the first-ever Emmy for Outstanding Music Supervision.

Fitting for a song called 'Clocks': Coldplay singer Chris Martin's great-great-grandfather was William Willett, the Englishman who campaigned to introduce British Summer Time — effectively the man who helped invent moving the clocks.
The Turu Anasi Remix appears on Nhii's 'The Secret Drums of Bwiti' EP, released on the Cosmic Awakenings label in 2020.
The remix stretches to just over six minutes at a downtempo 104 BPM in B minor.
Remixer Turu Anasi is an electronic producer based in Dnipro, Ukraine, known for weaving multicultural, ethno-tinged melodies into downtempo and organic house.
The title nods to Bwiti, a spiritual tradition of forest-dwelling peoples of Gabon centred on the iboga plant used to reach trance states.
The moniker Nhii is an initialism for 'No Human Is Illegal,' reflecting the DJ's borderless, globe-spanning approach to electronic music.

Jiandro is a Dutch producer-turned-artist (his father is from Curaçao) who built his following by chopping nostalgic pop and R&B into short, hook-driven tracks for TikTok and YouTube before scoring his own breakout single.
'Confess Your Love,' featuring vocalist ola.wav, became Jiandro's viral breakthrough in 2025, soundtracking a wave of TikTok edits and a trending dance built around its hook.
Like many TikTok-born hits, the track lives in dozens of unofficial mutations — sped-up, slowed and remix versions circulate alongside the original across Spotify, YouTube and Audiomack.
Fake Moses is a DJ and producer from Tbilisi, Georgia, who describes his output as fresh, bouncy house for any dancing occasion.
'See The Sea' is the title track of a self-released two-song EP (paired with 'Morning Coffee') that came out on 10 July 2024.
It's a long-form dance cut, running roughly seven and a half minutes.
Bandcamp tags the EP across a spread of house styles at once — deep, tech, minimal, funky and groovy house.

James Murphy wrote the song about a marriage breakup, calling it 'music of desperation' — yet he deliberately wanted it to be 'really beautiful,' and nearly cut it from the album until drummer Pat Mahoney talked him into keeping it.
The Gary Numan-style lead is one synth patch doing two jobs at once: a mellow triangle-wave oscillator carries the melody while a lower rectangular-wave oscillator plays the bassline.
Building the song, Murphy drew on his 1980s heroes — 'Sweet Dreams'-era Eurythmics, Bronski Beat and early OMD — topped with a Jimmy Somerville-style falsetto over an acid-house beat.
The song was licensed to the video game FIFA 11, giving it a life on soundtracks well beyond the dance floor.
Rolling Stone ranked 'I Can Change' No. 17 on its best-songs-of-2010 list, and indie artist Ezra Furman later recorded a stripped-back acoustic cover.

The lyrics are almost documentary: they describe a real emergency after Sofi Tukker's Sophie Hawley-Weld broke her foot during a live set in Australia, forcing the duo to fly home in the middle of their tour.
Released in September 2020, 'Emergency' saw Sofi Tukker team up with fellow producers Novak and YAX.X during a period when injury and the pandemic had grounded their touring entirely.

The song was road-tested before release: it became an audience favourite in the daily livestream DJ sets Sofi Tukker ran throughout lockdown, then got an official studio release once fans had already fallen for it.
The official video is an animated, video-game-inspired piece directed by Jared Asher Harris — a nod to the duo's love of playful, screen-native visuals.

'Emergency' was one of the tracks that grew out of Sofi Tukker's remarkable quarantine run of 100-plus daily livestreams (their 'Freak Fam' shows), which also birthed the companion lockdown single 'House Arrest.'

This is a fan-made megamix by Adamusic (Adam Wright), an LA-based mashup artist originally from Grand Rapids, Michigan, who built a following of over a million by weaving current and older hits into single seamless mixes.
Adamusic's mashup reputation carried into the mainstream — in 2025 he became the newest face of Apple Music's DJ Mix series, launching with a 25-track set of his own self-made mashups.

The core track being remixed, Dua Lipa's 'Dance the Night,' was written for the Barbie film by Dua Lipa, Caroline Ailin, Andrew Wyatt and Mark Ronson — and Ronson landed the whole job after receiving a text that simply said 'Barbie?'

On the original 'Dance the Night,' nearly every part was performed live rather than programmed — everything except the drums — and Mark Ronson wrote its chord progression on his Rhodes electric piano.
Dua Lipa and Mark Ronson substantially re-wrote 'Dance the Night' after watching the actual Barbie dance sequence, reshaping the song so it would lock to the on-screen action.
'Sacatela' started as a drunken in-joke — friends messing around singing the word 'sacatela' with a guitar — and the band liked the phrase so much they built an entire song around it.
It was the lead single from Teatro Lucido, La Femme's first album sung entirely in Spanish — a leap that grew out of touring Latin America and Spain.
The music video was directed by Ilan Zerrouki and shot in the French Riviera city of Nice, packing in a crowd of the band's rotating members.
The band coined a concept for the video's theme — 'Sacatelism' — which they define as being about unacknowledged desires and dreams you never chase.
La Femme are a French band formed in Biarritz in 2010 by Sacha Got and Marlon Magnée, known for blending krautrock, '60s surf and psych-pop; the Spanish title roughly translates as 'take it out.'

Zeca Veloso wrote 'Todo Homem' in 2015 as only his second-ever composition; built around the tender idea that every man needs a mother, it uses images like an umbilical cord to capture a bond that never truly fades.

The song was Zeca's recorded debut and public breakout, unveiled on the 2018 'Ofertorio' tour where his father Caetano Veloso reunited on stage with all three sons — Moreno, Zeca and Tom — before audiences topping 40,000.
The original is anchored by Zeca's fragile falsetto and a solo piano introduction so beloved that live audiences would applaud the moment he began playing it — before he sang a note.
'Todo Homem' reached millions of Brazilians as the opening theme of TV Globo's 2018 prime-time telenovela 'Onde Nascem os Fortes,' the placement that turned the family song into a national hit.
In August 2022, Brazilian producers Antdot and Maz reworked the ballad into a seven-minute organic-house version — keeping Zeca's vocal but wrapping it in dreamy piano leads and a 124 BPM groove.

'Do It Like This' is an upbeat confidence anthem: rather than the darker mental-health themes Daphne Willis is known for, it's a call to make a grand entrance, live in the moment and enjoy yourself without worrying who's watching.

Though it never charted, the 2018 single became Willis's most commercially licensed track — by her own account landing more than ten major international sync placements — and she credits it as a key driver of her exposure.
In April 2025 Willis revisited the song with 'Do It Like This — Reimagined,' a fresh re-recording she co-produced with songwriter-producer Sophie Delila, about seven years after the original.
The track turns up in 'The SpongeBob Movie: Sponge on the Run' (2020), scoring the sequence where SpongeBob and Patrick blow off their mission to gorge, ride rides and gamble through a glitzy detour.
Pub-quiz gold: alongside placements for Samsung, Xfinity and the TV show Empire, the song has reportedly served as the on-hold telephone music for Royal Caribbean Cruise Lines.

Despite its throwback soul-jazz feel, 'Got To Be Mine' is an original, not a cover: it was co-written by vocalist Evangeline and Jack Stratton (Vulfmon), the Vulfpeck founder, and released on his 2024 solo album 'Dot.'
The breezy, flute-forward arrangement is the work of multi-instrumentalist Aaron Kruziki, whose winds and orchestration led critics to dub the track a 'fluffy and flute-y' jam.
The light, poppy tune hides a heavyweight rhythm section: Vulfpeck's Joe Dart on bass, acclaimed jazz drummer Nate Smith on drums, and in-demand session guitarist Ella Feingold on guitar.
In the official video, Stratton and Evangeline stroll and dance along a graffiti-covered Los Angeles pedestrian bridge shot through a wide fisheye lens, with choreography by Evangeline herself.

'Vulfmon' isn't just a solo alias but a character: Stratton invented the persona of an old-school German record producer, which is why his Bandcamp releases are cheekily tagged as coming from Halle, Germany.
'Boom Shaka Laka' was written and composed by Italian dance producer Mauro Vay (credited on release metadata as 'Mauro Vai'), listed as both writer and composer.
Boom Face's 'Boom Shaka Laka' was released on 15 March 2013 as a six-track EP on the Italian dance imprint Bit Records, part of The Saifam Group.
The composer remixed his own track: one of the EP's featured versions is the 'DJ Mauro Vay & Luke GF Remix.'
The track had a second life in 2016 when a fresh 'Marco Veneziano Remix' surfaced on the Saifam compilation 'Addicted To Latin.'
An official music video for the track was posted to YouTube in 2013.

The whole song grew out of a single word: the band wanted to echo Brigitte Bardot's 'Contact,' in which she repeats one word over and over, so they asked what word they could loop endlessly, landed on 'repeat,' and built the track around it.
'Boyfriend (Repeat)' was Confidence Man's very first single, released in 2016; it won Electronic Song of the Year at the 2017 Queensland Music Awards and even cracked the Belgian (Wallonia) chart.

The joke is baked into the arrangement: Janet Planet's deadpan lead — dressing down a clingy partner — is answered by a detached male chorus chanting 'repeat,' mockingly voicing the needy boyfriend himself.
The track found a second life on screen in Netflix's 2018 rom-com 'To All the Boys I've Loved Before,' soundtracking a cafeteria scene as Lara Jean and Peter go public.

Pub-quiz gold: the band's two masked members took their aliases — Reggie Goodchild and Clarence McGuffie — off real headstones in a graveyard in Roma, rural Queensland; the real Goodchild's daughter later got in touch.
The artist, Jade Rose, builds the whole trance track live in Strudel — a browser-based live-coding environment she helps maintain — with the music re-shaping on the fly as she edits the code.
Her 'from scratch' coding videos are more than demos: the released track 'In the Beginning, there was Trance' first came to life inside one such YouTube live-coding session.
Before live coding, Rose trained as a luthier, learning to build string instruments by hand and to understand the physical acoustics of wood and air.
She describes her method as weaving 'musical fractals,' inspired by the cyclic patterns of North Indian classical music and of textiles.
Her sets look so finished that viewers have mistaken the live-coded performances for a polished pre-produced music video — only realising afterward that the sound was being generated live.

Singer-guitarist Sandrushka Petrova has said the band's concept album was sparked by watching the film 'Joker,' which set her reflecting on the hopelessness and declining mental health of the modern world.
'After Destruction' is the fourth studio album from the long-running Mexican art-rock band, whose underground sound folds together punk, shoegaze, prog and cabaret.

The band wrote a fictional machine called 'The DAK' into their line-up — an automaton meant to turn emotional pain into art, which surfaces through spoken interludes on the record and in their live show.
Across the album's videos, director Persia Campbell built one deliberately artificial world of pink hues, vintage TV sets and plastic flowers to mirror the songs' themes of disillusionment.
Beneath the sci-fi story, the album works as satire of the modern wellness industry, imagining a simulated reality that sells '37 different pre-programmed Enlightenment Bubbles.'
The Acos Coolkas Remix of AN-2's 'Lazy Sun' was released in September 2015 on Theomatic Records, an independent label from St. Petersburg, Russia.
Remixers Acos CoolKAs are the duo Konstantin Atomas and Vasiliy Basalaev from Omsk, Siberia — around 2,500 km east of Moscow.
The pair are devoted to analog synthesizers for their 'deep cosmic sound,' with Vasiliy having even tried building his own.
The remix is a seven-minute journey clocking in around 116 BPM in A minor.
AN-2 and Acos CoolKAs share a reciprocal remix relationship on Theomatic — AN-2 has in turn reworked Acos CoolKAs's 'Skyline.'
Lizzo has said the megamix's centrepiece, 'Juice,' is about looking in the mirror, loving what you see and letting everyone know it — a feel-good anthem with a protest-song heart.

The mashup is the work of Adamusic — Adam Wright, an LA-based mashup artist from Grand Rapids, Michigan, best known for year-end 'megamixes' that stitch together 100-plus songs; this Juice edit landed in April 2020.
'Juice' was produced by Ricky Reed with a full live band and a three-piece horn section, giving it a retro-funk sound built for an early-'80s dancefloor.
Lizzo's 'Juice' video leans hard into '80s kitsch, parodying Jane Fonda workout tapes, QVC shopping channels and soft-focus lotion adverts.
This is a fan megamix, not an official single — it layers Lizzo's 'Juice' with hits by Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Dua Lipa and Doja Cat, none of whom actually released the track.
This is the official cinematic video for Eurielle's self-titled song 'Eurielle,' a track from her debut album 'Arcadia,' published in March 2016.
Eurielle (real name Lauren Walker, raised in Yorkshire) is a classically trained soprano who studied at London's Royal Academy of Music and began recording 'Arcadia' before she graduated.
'Arcadia' was self-released in December 2015 and produced in collaboration with Ryan Louder.
Her voice has featured in screen and game projects including Downton Abbey, Enola Holmes, Shazam! and Lords of the Fallen, and her music has been sampled by artists such as Migos.
At age 13 she was approached by Sony Music to be developed as a 'Charlotte Church alternative' — an offer she turned down to keep pursuing her classical studies.
The track grew out of Soulwax's touring 'Transient Program for Drums and Machinery' show; rather than assembling it in the studio, the band captured the whole album in a single continuous live take.
It appears on 'From DEEWEE' (2017), which won Album of the Year at Belgium's Music Industry Awards and came out on the Ghent duo's own DEEWEE label, named after their studio.
That one take was recorded at DEEWEE Studio in Ghent on 7 February 2017, with the full band and three drummers playing simultaneously.

The official video isn't a narrative but a document of the drums-and-machinery installation, filmed live at 3 Mills Studios in London and showing the song assembled from its thunderous multi-drummer intro upward.
One of the three drummers powering the track is Iggor Cavalera, co-founder of Brazilian thrash-metal legends Sepultura.

'Friday,' by Manchester artist Xenya Genovese (aka Freak Slug), sketches a complicated relationship — watching someone drift through their struggles and deciding to pull away despite still caring for them.
The song was released on 13 August 2020 and later gathered onto her 'Videos EP' that October.
Freak Slug largely self-produces, working in a lo-fi dream-pop haze whose intimate, double-tracked vocals critics often compare to Elliott Smith.
Genovese first drew wider attention when HBO's skateboarding series 'Betty' featured her cover of a Joy Division song.
She keeps tight creative control of Freak Slug — writing, producing and self-directing her own music videos, and preferring to work alone to keep everything authentic to her vision.
The song this fan megamix is built on, Doja Cat's 'Say So,' began as an album cut on 2019's 'Hot Pink'; its lyrics are a flirtation, nudging someone she's clicked with to finally make the first move.
'Say So' was produced by Dr. Luke under the alias 'Tyson Trax,' blending 1970s funk and disco with pop-rap.
The track exploded thanks to a TikTok dance created by teenager Haley Sharpe; Doja Cat then cast Sharpe in the song's roller-rink, '70s-styled video directed by Hannah Lux Davis.
After a remix featuring Nicki Minaj, 'Say So' topped the Billboard Hot 100 — a first-ever No. 1 for both artists, and the first time two female rappers led the chart together.
That chart-topper also broke a record: it gave Nicki Minaj her first Hot 100 No. 1 on her 109th charted title — the longest wait to the summit in the chart's history.
The band's name comes from their very first song, 'Fully Rehearsed,' which they wrote as a Christmas gift for their older sister.
BIG SIS began as a just-for-fun joke project, but after their second song was warmly received they decided to keep going.
They call their genre 'cheeky dance pop,' listing influences from Daft Punk, Lady Gaga, Doechii and Doja Cat to Jim Carrey, SpongeBob SquarePants and Elmo.
'Yay Yomes' went viral and won the act a wave of new fans; a 2025 remix later added Harrisun, Flex Grizzly and LINUS AK.
The single was released on 19 May 2023, and is offered on Bandcamp in hi-res 24-bit audio.

The band framed the song as the closing tale of their album 'From The Pyre,' set in what they called the 'sinister mythworld' of Los Angeles — Hollywood as 'the ultimate fairytale' full of Grimm-like characters chasing their own hero's journey.
It was recorded with producer Animesh Raval at Church Studios in Crouch End, London, and was the very last song the band finished during the album sessions.
The video, directed by Sinclair Bryant, is a love letter to classic cinema — nodding to Hollywood noir sirens, slasher-movie characters and the camp aesthetic of filmmaker John Waters.
The band first performed it live at London's O2 Academy Brixton in December 2025, before playing it at Madrid's Mad Cool festival the following July.
The track arrived as a new song on the deluxe edition of the band's 2025 album 'From The Pyre.'

Icona Pop made the song after leaving Los Angeles to ride out the COVID lockdown back home in Stockholm, reconnecting with their electronic roots — Aino Jawo noting the irony that 'the quietest period' of their careers produced such danceable music.
The duo's vocals sit atop Grammy-nominated Galantis's production, built from windswept breakdowns, euphoric synth stabs and throbbing choruses.
Released in February 2023 on Ultra Records, it became track 8 on Icona Pop's album 'Club Romantech,' which earned a 'generally favourable' 75/100 on Metacritic.
The clip on the YouTube release is an official visualizer put out through Ultra Records rather than a narrative music video.
The track spawned a run of club remixes, including versions by Moyo and by Sangmoo & Noisy Choice.
'Seahorse' is distributed free through YouTube's Audio Library, tagged World / Happy, running about 2:38 and cleared for use with no attribution required.
The Rondo Brothers are a San Francisco duo — Jim Greer and Brandon Arnovick — who met in 1998 but only began making music together in 2003, going on to score a run of NFL commercials.
They produced 'Chin Music For The Unsuspecting Hero,' which appeared on the single release of Foster the People's 'Pumped Up Kicks.'
The pair came up through producer Dan the Automator's circle: Greer played keys in the original Dr. Octagon live band, and Arnovick played guitar with Deltron 3030 and Lovage.
Their music has appeared on screen in TV series such as True Blood and Billions and in the documentary 'My Kid Could Paint That.'
'Shake It' arrived in early 2023 as a joint release between Insomniac Records and Defected's D4 D4NCE imprint.
Deeper Purpose came up with the vocal hook himself, then enlisted a friend to turn it into a male-female duet, echoing his earlier track 'Party Diva.'
He road-tested 'Shake It' live at San Diego's CRSSD Festival in September 2022, months before the record's release.
Deeper Purpose is Stephen Galloway of Croydon, London, whose remix of Piero Pirupa's 'Everybody's Free' was 2021's longest-running Beatport Tech House No. 1.
The tech-house cut runs at 126 BPM, built around a grooving bassline and a hypnotic spoken vocal.
'Do It, Do It Again' is the English rewrite of Carrà's 1976 Italian smash 'A far l'amore comincia tu,' written by Franco Bracardi and Daniele Pace and produced by Gianni Boncompagni.
The English version reached No. 9 on the UK Singles Chart in 1978 — and remained the Italian star's only UK chart entry until 2024. It also hit No. 20 in Canada.
Carrà cut the same song in a remarkable spread of languages — Spanish, German and French — while a German cover, Tony Holiday's 'Tanze Samba mit mir,' reached No. 4 on its own.
The tune found a new audience in 2011 when French DJ Bob Sinclar sampled it for the club hit 'Far l'amore,' which reached No. 6 in Italy.
Sinclar's reworking soundtracks a memorable rooftop-party scene in Paolo Sorrentino's 'The Great Beauty' (2013), which won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
'Inner Light' appears on Baldelli's 2015 album 'Cosmic Temple Chapter 1,' co-produced with Mattia Dallara and featuring lyrics by Francesca Amati, on the Italian label Cinedelic.
Baldelli is widely regarded as the godfather of 'cosmic' disco, the sound he forged as resident DJ of the Cosmic club, which opened on Lake Garda in April 1979.

His cosmic DNA came from a radical booth technique: playing records at the 'wrong' speed (a 45 spun at 33), blending psychedelic rock, fusion, African music and new wave, and layering a Korg drum machine and a Yamaha CS10 synth.
The track was given a fresh spin by producer Alkalino, who reworked it into an italo-disco remix for 'Cosmic Temple – The Remixes.'
Baldelli's cosmic style became so sought-after that fans travelled across Europe to buy his mixtapes, which he crafted using four turntables and a Revox tape machine.
Logan Spaleta is a Saratoga Springs, New York singer-songwriter (Williams College class of 2028) who has written over 100 songs, several released on Spotify and Apple Music.
He released 'Broken Glass' together with the single 'summer camp' on 5 September 2023.
Spaleta described 'Broken Glass' as having a darker, more cutting-edge complexion, pairing thoughtful lyrics with powerful orchestration as a step toward more mature material.
His parents raised him on 1980s music and started him on piano at age six; by nine he was performing songs he'd heard at home by Billy Joel and John Nilsen.
The clip for this track is the official lyric video for 'Broken Glass.'
